big_idea: Social success comes less from raw charisma than from a set of specific, learnable verbal and nonverbal techniques that make other people feel noticed, valued, and comfortable in your presence.

tool.label: The flooding smile
tool.text: Instead of smiling reflexively the instant you meet someone, pause a beat, take in their face, then let a warm smile spread slowly across yours; the slight delay reads as genuine and personal rather than automatic.
tool.note: One of Lowndes' opening first-impression moves, used alongside related nonverbal tricks like Sticky Eyes and the Big Baby Pivot.

ideas.title: Sticky eyes
ideas.text: Hold your gaze on the speaker a moment after they've finished talking, signaling full attention rather than a wandering mind.

ideas.title: Big baby pivot
ideas.text: Turn your entire body toward whoever is speaking to you, the way an infant fully turns toward a parent's voice.

ideas.title: Whozit opener
ideas.text: Break into a new group or approach a stranger by asking a low-risk question like who's that; it's an easy, natural entry point.

ideas.title: Parroting
ideas.text: When you're stuck for a response, repeat back the last few words someone said as a question, buying time while signaling you were listening.

ideas.title: Grapevine glory
ideas.text: Say something complimentary about someone to a third party, trusting it will circulate back; indirect praise often lands harder than direct praise.

ideas.title: The munching mingler mistake
ideas.text: Eat before networking events so your hands stay free and you're not stuck hovering near the buffet, avoiding the isolation trap.

try_it: At your next introduction, deliberately delay your smile one beat before letting it spread.
Practice sticky eyes in three conversations this week: hold eye contact a moment after the other person stops talking.
Use the whozit opener at one social or work event to start a conversation with someone you don't know.
Say something genuinely positive about a colleague to a third person and notice if it circulates back.
best_for: People anxious about small talk or networking events
Readers who want concrete body-language scripts to rehearse
less_useful: Readers wanting psychological theory or research backing
Anyone put off by techniques that can feel performative if used insincerely
